To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
monoclonal antibodies that recognize epitopes outside the HLH domain of myogenin interfere with the interaction of myogenin with DNA.
monoclonal antimyogenic antibodies define epitopes spanning the molecule outside the HLh region and some of these epitopes interfere with the binding to DNA of myogenic heterodimers.
we have developed a panel monoclonal antibodies to myogenin and used these antibodies to define epitopes outside of the bHLh domain that interfere with protein-DNA interactions of myogenin.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and characterization of a panel of monoconal antibodies against myogenin.
the use of monoclonal antimyogenic antibodies to define myogenic regulatory protein structure-function relationships.
the production and use of monoclonal antimyogemin antibodies.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the monoclonals against epitopes outside of the HLH domain interfere with the binding to DNA and/or the binding of myogenic heterodimer.
these antibodies are very useful in the analysis of myogenin structure and function.
the monoclonal antibodies recognize epitopes that span the entire molecule outside of the bHLh domain, and that some of the epitopes may play a role in protein-DNA and protein-protein interactions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the monoclonal antibodies we have produced against myogenin recognize epitopes outside the dimerization domain, some of which interfere with protein-protein interactions and others with protein-DNA interactions.
the binding of antibodies to myogenin epitopes outside the HLH domain can interfere with protein-protein interactions and/or with protein-DNA interactions, depending on the epitope.
monoclonal antibodies directed against myogenin can be used to map the surfaces of the protein involved in DNA-binding, dimerization and protein-protein interactions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
monoclonal antibodies can be used to probe the structure and function of bHLH proteins, even when the epitopes they recognize are not in the HLH domain.
monoclonal antibody epitopes are often located in regions that are not directly involved in the function of the molecule.
antibodies against myogenin can be used to probe protein interactions and to map the epitopes of other antibodies.
